Batch 1, 9/17/26: the twenty best-covered brands in the Index.
malbon: Malbon Golf is the most-covered brand in this Index by a distance, and it started as an Instagram mood board. Erica and Stephen Malbon launched it in Los Angeles in 2017 having never worked in either sport or retail — her previous business was a massage studio in the city — and the account existed well before any clothing did.

The company built menswear first and took years to add a full women's line, which is unusual for a brand whose entire early identity was aesthetic rather than technical. What it sells now runs from soft knits and relaxed tailoring through to the collaborations and limited runs that generate most of the noise around it. If you are trying to understand why golf clothing stopped apologising for itself somewhere around 2018, this is the company the rest of the category was reacting to.
manors: Manors is a London label built by two school friends, Jojo Regan and Luke Davies, who spent a summer playing golf dressed nothing like golfers and decided that technical apparel was an answer to a question neither of them had asked. It arrived in 2019 with Nick Watts as Fashion Director, aiming the whole look at the game's golden age.

Then the brand went quiet on social in the spring of 2023, and what came back was a technical golf company — which makes the current rail unusually interesting, because both halves of the argument are still hanging on it. The Merino Tech line runs a hoodie at $305, a windbreaker at $292 and a crewneck at $244, all of them wool rather than synthetic fleece. Beside them sits a buttoned Primaloft cardigan at $217, about as old-fashioned a silhouette as the game offers.
jones-sports-co: George Jones was a forty-year-old Portland taxi driver who sewed the first of these bags in his basement in 1971. The design has barely moved since, and what makes it good is subtractive: no legs, no cart strap, no panelling breaking the surface.

The middle of the story is the part Jones Sports Co. tends to skip. George sold up in 1990, and the buyers set about making the bag more like everyone else's, which is a strange thing to do to a bag whose whole argument was that it was not. By the early 2000s the label had all but disappeared. The Lemman family bought it back in 2011 with Chris Carnahan, found there was almost nothing left to buy, and rebuilt the pattern from old examples gathered around Portland. The Original is priced on material rather than construction: $125 in Burnt Clay, $175 in nylon, $215 in vegan leather, one 2.9-pound body and one three-way divider throughout.
fyfe-golf: Fyfe makes headcovers to order in Harris Tweed and tartan, and the house construction is the thing to look at rather than the pattern. Every cover pairs a body cloth with a contrast accent band. That band is a separate piece of cloth sewn in, not a printed stripe, which leaves an edge you can feel through the wool, and the lining is plush fleece in a colour chosen against the outside.

The naming follows the Scottish coast and the islands — Rothesay for the harbour town on Bute, Arran in oatmeal with a green band, Dunbar in duck egg drawn from the East Lothian rock shelves, Black Grouse in houndstooth with a red lining. Beyond the tweed, Fyfe has cut covers from RAF flight suits and Augusta coveralls, which is a different kind of sourcing altogether and the reason the brand turns up in conversations about provenance rather than pattern.
seamus: Seamus began with a headcover that had worn through. Akbar Chisti's father had given him one from a famous links club; his wife Megan, then a womenswear designer at Pendleton Woolen Mills, sewed a replacement. Bandon Dunes, where Akbar spent a college summer caddying, placed the first wholesale order, and fifteen years on everything is still cut and sewn in Beaverton, Oregon.

The work that made the name came in 2016, when Matt Kuchar asked for American flag covers for every member of the United States Ryder Cup team: thirteen stripes cut by hand and fifty stars embroidered on each one. The civilian version, the Patriot, is $140. A licensed Pendleton line closes the loop back to Megan's old employer, and a canvas corner of the catalogue embroidered with pop-culture figures sits at $155 and stays permanently on the bestsellers page.
sugarloaf-social-club: Sugarloaf Social Club was a group chat before it was a company — a few college roommates graduating in 2011 — and it now covers a wider spread of prices than anyone else in independent golf while sounding like one voice across all of it. A MacKenzie sailcloth bag at $1,400 and a paper fan at $14 read as the same brand, which is harder than it looks.

The course it takes its name from no longer exists. Sugarloaf Mountain, in Minneola, Florida, was the first Coore & Crenshaw design in the state, laid out over 250-odd feet of elevation change, and it opened in 2008 straight into the financial crisis and never recovered. One thing to know about the ownership: the brand sits under Pro Shop, Inc., which also owns Skratch and GolfWRX and has taken roughly $20 million in backing from the PGA Tour and Powerhouse Capital.
gumtree-golf: Gumtree Golf & Nature Club sews out of a Greenpoint studio in Brooklyn, run by a Melbourne transplant who put the gum leaf in the name. The signature product is a headcover cut from wetsuit herringbone neoprene, which starts around $105 and is a material nobody else in golf is working in.

What happens when that operation builds a full wardrobe is that almost none of it screams golf. There are no polos and no moisture-wicking copy. Instead: barrel jeans made in Portugal at $200, a cropped mohair sweater handmade in New York at $250, a short-sleeve shirt cut from a vintage cotton lace roll and limited to fifteen pieces at $285, and a ripstop Beachcomber short at $125. The brand also runs multi-day ecology retreats in the Catskills, which tells you where the Nature half of the name comes from.
sentinel-golf: Sentinel builds carry bags in Minneapolis at prices that leave no room to hide, and the range is organised by material rather than by feature list. The Basecamp Walker takes the MacKenzie Walker pattern — a shape that arrived essentially finished in the 1990s — and rebuilds it in black Dyneema composite: matte, papery, entirely leather-free, made to order on roughly six weeks at $890.

Above it sits the same pattern in nubuck from Sørensen, the Danish tannery founded in 1973, at $1,750 on eight weeks with no customisation and all sales final. The cheaper end is a project with Chicago's 1733: a duffle and a tote at $320 in triple-layer construction, built around a Saltex nylon that is woven in Japan, salt-bathed and then heat-treated, with hand-tied paracord pulls.
students-golf: Students Golf launched in 2022 under the line “For Golfers Who Study The Game”, and the conceit runs all the way through the catalogue rather than sitting on a hangtag. Pieces are named for campus life — the Calculus pant, the Librarian polo, the 1st String sweater — and the visual language borrows from varsity graphics and vintage Americana rather than from performance sportswear.

The range is deep enough to be genuinely hard to shop: more than 500 SKUs across polos, trousers, shorts, outerwear, hats, headcovers and accessories. The Course Studies line is where the technical work sits, with the Librarian polo at $98 in a micro-waffle knit with anti-odour and UV treatment, tech zip polos alongside it at the same price, and the Ledgewood at $105. The collaboration bench is unusually deep for a label this young.
walker-golf-things: Walker Golf Things comes off the Gold Coast and is run by Jack Fardell, a professional skateboarder, which explains more about the graphics than any brand statement would. The name is a Nicklaus reference. The collaboration list — adidas, Wahine, Coopers — is broad for an Australian label this size.

The interesting production decision is on the Blooming Grounds knit polo at $120: the artwork is knitted into the body as a full custom jacquard rather than printed on top of it, so sky, treeline, creek and fairway are structural. The hand-drawn version of the same scene runs across the back of a $50 cotton tee, which is the cheapest way in. Elsewhere there is a seersucker camp-collar shirt at $110 scattered with embroidered golfers, and the Featherlite polo at $100 is the most conventionally golf-looking thing they make.
devereux-golf: Devereux exists because Robert Brunner could not find what he wanted to wear. He had read geology at TCU and gone into the gas industry, hated it, and taken a year at a Los Angeles fashion school before turning up with a golf line and a pitch for his brother Will, who took operations. Scottsdale, 2013.

The name is family. Asked about it in the brand's first year, Robert did not dress it up — it is his grandmother's name, she was turning ninety that March, and they wanted to keep it in the family. The clothes were cut relaxed well before that was normal in golf, and the outerwear is the clearest expression of it: the Devco twill jacket at $138, an anorak at $148 that folds down small enough to sit in a bag all winter, and the Thunderbird bomber at $134.
metalwood-studio: Metalwood Studio is Cole Young's Los Angeles operation, and it mines the Y2K tour aesthetic so precisely that it became the blueprint a lot of golf nostalgia has followed since. Most of the brand's biggest moments arrive with somebody else's name alongside it.

The adidas partnership is the clearest case. The MC70 golf shoe at $200 puts a deco-stitched leather upper drawn from 1970s football boots onto a modern golf chassis, and dropped through CONFIRMED. The stranger and better one is the Predator Sala Vino at $150 — an indoor-soccer silhouette rebuilt in shaggy suede and glossy burgundy overlays for adidas Skateboarding, by a golf brand, which had a queue down La Brea in January. A baggy nineties-cut trouser at $150 and a cabretta glove at $35 round the collaboration out.
left-of-field-golf: Left of Field works surf and skate silhouettes onto the golf course from Sydney, and the collections are named after stretches of the Australian coastline. That is a working method rather than a naming gimmick: the reference points are real places and the design usually follows a trip.

Elements is the flagship technical line, drawn after the brand went to Barnbougle. The Elements polo at $105 carries a yardage print from that collection; the Bass polo at the same price is named for Bass Strait, where Barnbougle's weather arrives from, and is deliberately black and unprinted. The Elements weather jacket at $143 is where the word technical earns itself — windproof, water-repellent, insulated front panel, YKK hardware. The Bridport crewneck at $165 takes its contrast panel from the paths winding between the fairways at the course, and Bridport is the town beside it.
birds-of-condor: Frankie Kimpton booked bands in Melbourne for Mushroom and surfed competitively at Byron Bay before he ever made a golf hat, and he has been unusually direct about not fitting in at driving ranges. He and Zoe Kimpton began with ten hats and a garage. The brand puts its founding at 2016, from an idea that turned up on lunch breaks at a Melbourne range a few years earlier, and it was exporting to South Korea, Japan and America inside its first year.

The name is a scoring term: four under par at one hole, which by the brand's own reckoning has never once been recorded in professional play. The commercial engine is simpler than the name: snapbacks at $50 carrying the crests of Tokyo Country Club and Osaka Country Club, neither of which is a real place. Between them, those two motifs occupy every slot in the top eleven of the brand's own bestseller list.
quiet-golf: Quiet Golf came out of the Museum of Peace & Quiet orbit, founded by Christion Lennon with Raul and Diego Diaz, and works from a flagship on Randolph Avenue in Costa Mesa. The crest is an owl. The proposition is in the name, and the most-repeated line about the clothes is that they carry the quietest logo in golf.

The range is built on cloth rather than graphics — Supima cotton polos made in Portugal, cashmere sweaters, linen trousers, corduroy jackets — alongside collaborations including an adidas Samba. Old Tom Capital backed the company in 2024 and led a later seed round, and it is carried by Nordstrom, Revolve and Shopbop. Current pieces run from a $55 garment-washed pocket tee through a $114 active-pique polo and a $130 pleated short to the $148 Monterey hoodie.
radry-golf: Radry is a Wisconsin artist's brand operating out of Sheboygan since 2018, and the order of operations matters: everything is drawn before it is stitched. The logo is a bird in a bucket hat, and the house characters carry more of the identity than any wordmark does.

The closest thing to a signature product is the Gang Gang headcover pair at $65 each, blade and mallet, cut in sage corduroy. Corduroy is a strange material for a headcover and it works, because the ribbed pile holds embroidery in a way leather cannot. The hoodies split the difference between loud and wearable: a black full-zip at $95 carrying a small embroidered smiley on the chest, and the Mouthful at $95 in off-white, its wordmark scattered in multicolour letters that read as a child's drawing from ten feet away.
mogshade: Mogshade makes headcovers and towels in Portugal, to order, on a lead time of about three weeks. The work is jacquard-woven rather than printed, which is the distinction that separates the brand from most of the headcover market and the reason the patterns hold their edges.

The references are specifically Portuguese. Azulejo takes its geometry from the hand-painted tiles covering Lisbon's facades. Deco Blue reads like something pulled off the wall of a 1920s hotel lobby, in blues and golds with a fleece lining and a leather accent. The most interesting line is Re.Weave, made from rescued high-quality fabrics woven in the mountain factories of the Serra da Estrela — the Churra Mono is named after the sheep breed native to that region and has a handwoven character you can feel through the wool. A waffle-weave towel runs alongside them in the same register.
mackenzie: MacKenzie has been making carry bags by hand in Oregon since 1985, and its position in the Index is unusual: it is at least as significant as a manufacturer for other people as it is as a brand of its own. Fyfe, Sugarloaf Social Club, Students, Miura and Bandon Dunes have all had bags built here.

The eight-inch top is the recurring shape, and the collaborations are where the range gets strange. The Sugarloaf bag in plain navy or Nantucket canvas at $875 is the one everything else is a variation on. The Hidden Gem at $850 is notable for carrying a water bottle holder, which the collaborator's own copy treats as a rare concession. A three-way with Students landed in February 2026 at $875 in 500D Cordura camo with merit patches and terry padding, and a white leather Double Seve reached $1,400.
eastside-golf: Eastside Golf was founded in Atlanta in 2019 by Olajuwon Ajanaku and Earl Cooper, and it brought streetwear construction and streetwear release cadence to a category that had neither. The Swingman — the figure mid-follow-through in a hoodie — does the work a logo normally does, and it is embroidered rather than printed.

The Jordan Brand collaborations are what most people know the label for, and they are the reason it turns up in conversations about golf's relationship with sneaker culture rather than with apparel. The core range is more approachable than the collaborations suggest: the Core Fleece Swingman hoodie sits around $88 in premium cotton with the script logo on the sleeve, which is the sensible entry point to a brand whose limited pieces move fast.
stitch-golf: STITCH has been making bags, travel covers and leather headcovers since 2012, working a line somewhere between Japanese minimalism and American engineering. The bags are the centre of it, and the SL2 is the one that defines the range.

The Gen 2, redesigned for 2026, sits at $398 with a refined stand mechanism, deeper pockets, a four-way top and dual carry straps. At just under five pounds it deliberately occupies the gap between a Sunday bag and a full stand bag — room for fourteen clubs and not much else — and comes in eight colourways. The headcovers work in a different register entirely: the Nice Roll at $78 is cobalt blue, scattered with candy-coloured dots under a small script, with no character and nothing to explain, which is rarer in headcovers than it sounds.
